full_text_en:
Michael Jeffrey Jordan v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, and Qiaodan Sports Co., Ltd. (Third Party) – Dispute over Administrative Dispute on Trademark

Ruling Summary

A “portrait” protected by the right of portrait shall be identifiable, and shall contain personal characteristics sufficient to enable the public to recognize the corresponding right holder, i.e., a specific natural person, so as to clearly refer to such corresponding right holder.

If a mark claimed to be protected by the right of portrait is not identifiable and cannot clearly refer to a specific natural person, it is difficult to establish on such mark the human dignity or personal interests that should be protected by law and that belong to a specific natural person.

If the mark claimed for protection of the right of portrait does not contain identifiable facial features, sufficient evidence shall be provided to prove that the mark contains other personal characteristics sufficient to reflect the corresponding natural person and is identifiable, so that the public can recognize that the mark clearly refers to such natural person.

Administrative Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2015) Zhi Xing Zi No. 332

Applicant for Retrial (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Michael Jeffrey Jordan, male, born on February 17, 1963, a national of the United States of America, residing in Chicago, Illinois, United States of America.

Agent ad litem: Tian Tian, lawyer of Shanghai Fangda (Beijing) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Qi Fang, lawyer of Shanghai Fangda (Beijing) Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce. Address: No. 1 Chama Nan Street, Xicheng District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Zhao Gang, Director of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Yang Shaowen, Examiner of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Wu Tong, Examiner of the Board.

Third Party at First Instance: Qiaodan Sports Co., Ltd. Address: Chendai Xibian Industrial Zone, Jinjiang City, Fujian Province, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Ding Guoxiong, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Ma Dongxiao, lawyer of Beijing Zhonglun Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wei Zhi, lawyer of Beijing Zhonglun Law Firm.

The Applicant for Retrial, Michael Jeffrey Jordan, dissatisfied with the Administrative Judgment (2015) Gao Xing (Zhi) Zhong Zi No. 965 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court in the case of dispute over administrative dispute on trademark against the Respondent, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board), and the Third Party at First Instance, Qiaodan Sports Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Qiaodan Company), filed an application for retrial with this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law to review this case and has now concluded the review.

Michael Jeffrey Jordan applied for retrial on the following grounds: (1) Article 100 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the General Principles of Civil Law) expressly provides for the right of portrait, therefore the right of portrait may constitute a "prior right" under Article 31 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China as amended in 2001 (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law). (2) The registration of Qiaodan Company's trademark No. 6020570, the graphic mark " [silhouette figure] " (hereinafter referred to as the disputed trademark), harmed the Applicant for Retrial's prior right of portrait and does not comply with Article 31 of the Trademark Law. 2.1 A photo of the Applicant for Retrial's sports image was published in "American Basketball Pictorial (Chinese International Edition)." This sports image gained widespread dissemination and attention, and the Applicant for Retrial has the right of portrait over it. 2.2 The disputed trademark design " [silhouette figure] " uses the Applicant for Retrial's sports image, which is likely to cause the relevant public to associate it with the Applicant for Retrial and lead to misidentification, thereby infringing on the Applicant for Retrial's right of portrait. 2.3 The Applicant for Retrial submitted "Michael Jordan and Qiaodan Sports Trademark Recognition Survey Report (Shanghai)" (hereinafter referred to as Survey Report 1) and "Michael Jordan and Qiaodan Sports Trademark Recognition Survey Report (National)" (hereinafter referred to as Survey Report 2). These two survey reports are sufficient to prove that products bearing the mark " [silhouette figure] " are likely to cause the relevant public to mistakenly believe that there is a specific relationship such as endorsement, authorization, license, or cooperation between Qiaodan Company and the Applicant for Retrial, and are likely to cause the relevant public to confuse the source of the goods. They can prove that in the public's perception, the mark " [silhouette figure] " has established a corresponding relationship with the Applicant for Retrial, and this corresponding relationship is significantly stronger than that between the mark and Qiaodan Company. 2.4 The protection of the right of portrait should not be premised on the Applicant for Retrial's active use of his sports image. 2.5 Whether the mark " [silhouette figure] " reflects the Applicant for Retrial's facial features is not a necessary condition for finding infringement on the right of portrait. (3) The first and second instance judgments erred in failing to find that Qiaodan Company had maliciously registered the disputed trademark. The Applicant for Retrial requested this Court: 1. to revoke the "Dispute Adjudication on Trademark No. 6020570 Graphic Trademark" (Shang Biao Ping Zi [2014] No. 52052) (hereinafter referred to as the Adjudication under Review) rendered by the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board; 2. to revoke the first and second instance judgments in this case.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board submitted its opinion that the Adjudication under Review had clear findings of fact, correct application of law, and was rendered in compliance with procedures, and requested the dismissal of the application for retrial.

Qiaodan Company submitted its opinion that: (1) The Applicant for Retrial does not have a right of portrait over the mark " [silhouette figure] ." 1.1 The silhouette of the mark is not completely identical to the body contour of the Applicant for Retrial's sports image. The action corresponding to the graphic is a common action in basketball and does not reflect the Applicant for Retrial's personal characteristics, and is unrelated to the Applicant for Retrial. 1.2 A portrait should clearly reflect the facial features of the subject, enabling the public to identify the portrait as belonging to the right holder. The mark " [silhouette figure] " lacks facial features, cannot correspond to the Applicant for Retrial, is not identifiable, and cannot receive protection of the right of portrait. (2) The survey reports 1 and 2 submitted by the Applicant for Retrial cannot prove his claims. 2.1 The two survey reports were completed by an independent third party, Beijing Horizon Market Research and Analysis Company (hereinafter referred to as Horizon Company), commissioned solely by the Applicant for Retrial, and the related fees were paid by the Applicant for Retrial. They lack neutrality and cannot serve as a basis for determining the facts of the case. 2.2 The sample of survey respondents in the two reports was unqualified, and the questions investigated were suggestive and leading, lacking objectivity, scientificity, and rationality. They are insufficient to prove a stable corresponding relationship between the mark " [silhouette figure] " and the Applicant for Retrial, and insufficient to prove that the public can identify the mark as the Applicant for Retrial. (3) The sports image claimed by the Applicant for Retrial is not well-known. Qiaodan Company has extensively promoted and used the mark " [silhouette figure] ," which has high visibility. The corresponding relationship between the mark and Qiaodan Company is significantly stronger than that with the Applicant for Retrial. (4) The new evidence provided by the Applicant for Retrial is irrelevant to this case.

With respect to the parties' retrial requests and the evidence submitted, this Court has investigated and determined the following evidence and facts related to the disputed issues in this case:

(I) Regarding the Applicant for Retrial's name

The name recorded in the Applicant for Retrial's passport is "Michael Jeffrey Jordan." In the Chinese translation provided by Beijing Baijia Translation Services Co., Ltd., it was translated as "迈克尔·杰弗里·乔丹." The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and Qiaodan Company did not object to this. Therefore, the Adjudication under Review and the first and second instance judgments erroneously found that the Applicant for Retrial's name was "迈克尔·乔丹 (Michael Jordan)," and this Court hereby corrects this error.

(II) Facts related to the sports image claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case

Issue No. 26 (January 15 to February 15, 1998) of "American Basketball Pictorial (Chinese International Edition)" published a photo of the Applicant for Retrial in a ball-holding sports action. In the photo, the Applicant for Retrial holds the ball horizontally with his right hand, stretches his left hand downward to the left, and his feet are off the ground. The body contour of his sports image is substantially identical to the disputed trademark design " [silhouette figure] ," but they are mirror images symmetrically reversed.

(III) Facts related to Survey Reports 1 and 2

The Applicant for Retrial commissioned Horizon Company, an independent third party, to produce Survey Reports 1 and 2 in June 2012. The attached question B1 in both reports was: "I will show you a picture (display the card of 'Qiaodan silhouette LOGO'). Who do you think the person in this picture is?" The conclusions of the two survey reports were: when displaying the silhouette LOGO of the Qiaodan Sports brand, without indicating options, 81% and 60.8% of respondents, respectively, believed it was the American basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan. The silhouette LOGO involved in the two reports is substantially identical to the disputed trademark design " [silhouette figure] ."

This Court finds that the disputed issues in this case are: (1) Whether the right of portrait claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case can constitute a "prior right" under Article 31 of the Trademark Law; (2) Whether the registration of the disputed trademark harms the right of portrait claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case.

(I) Whether the right of portrait claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case can constitute a "prior right" under Article 31 of the Trademark Law

Article 31 of the Trademark Law provides: "No application for trademark registration shall harm the existing prior rights of others." This Court holds that prior rights for which the Trademark Law has special provisions shall be protected in accordance with such special provisions. For prior rights that are not specifically provided for in the Trademark Law but should be protected under the General Principles of Civil Law, the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Tort Liability Law), and other laws, and that were lawfully enjoyed by civil subjects as civil rights or civil interests before the filing date of the disputed trademark, protection shall be granted in accordance with this general provision. Article 18 of the "Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases on Trademark Authorization and Confirmation," effective as of March 1, 2017, also provides: "Prior rights include civil rights or other lawful interests that the party enjoyed before the filing date of the trademark in dispute."

Regarding the right of portrait claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case, Article 100 of the General Principles of Civil Law provides: "Citizens have the right of portrait; without their consent, no one may use their portraits for profit." Article 2, Paragraph 2 of the Tort Liability Law provides: "The civil rights and interests referred to in this Law include rights of life, health, name, reputation, honor, portrait, and other personal and property rights." According to the above provisions, the right of portrait claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case can constitute a "prior right" under Article 31 of the Trademark Law.

(II) Whether the registration of the disputed trademark harms the right of portrait claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case

The Applicant for Retrial contends that the disputed trademark design " [silhouette figure] " is substantially identical to the body contour of the Applicant for Retrial's sports image in the photo, thereby harming his right of portrait. This Court holds that this ground for retrial cannot be established for the following specific reasons:

First, pursuant to the relevant provisions of the General Principles of Civil Law and the Tort Liability Law, the right of portrait is an important personal right enjoyed by natural persons. Protecting the right of portrait of natural persons is of great significance for maintaining their human dignity and protecting their personal interests. The "portrait" protected by the right of portrait is a visual reflection of the physical characteristics of a specific natural person. The public identifies and refers to the corresponding natural person through the "portrait" and can thereby distinguish that natural person from others. This Court holds that, given the nature of the right of portrait and the portrait itself, the "portrait" protected by the right of portrait shall be identifiable and shall contain personal characteristics sufficient to enable the public to recognize the corresponding right holder, i.e., a specific natural person, so as to clearly refer to such corresponding right holder. If a mark claimed to be protected by the right of portrait is not identifiable and cannot clearly refer to a specific natural person, it is difficult to establish on such mark the human dignity or personal interests that should be protected by law and that belong to a specific natural person.

Second, from the perspective of the public's cognitive habits and characteristics, the facial features of a natural person are the most important personal characteristics of their physical appearance. Under normal circumstances, the public can recognize and distinguish a specific natural person through their facial features. If the mark claimed for protection of the right of portrait does not contain identifiable facial features, sufficient evidence shall be provided to prove that the mark contains other personal characteristics sufficient to reflect the corresponding natural person and is identifiable, so that the public can recognize that the mark clearly refers to such natural person.

Third, regarding the right of portrait claimed by the Applicant for Retrial in this case. The photo of the Applicant for Retrial's sports image clearly reflects his facial features, body shape, jersey number, and other personal characteristics. The public can unambiguously identify the natural person in the photo as the Applicant for Retrial. Therefore, the Applicant for Retrial has the right of portrait over the sports image in the photo. However, regarding the disputed trademark design " [silhouette figure] ," although the silhouette is substantially identical to the mirror image of the body contour of the Applicant for Retrial's sports image in the photo, the mark is merely a black silhouette cutout. Apart from the body contour, it contains no personal characteristics related to the Applicant for Retrial. Moreover, the Applicant for Retrial does not have any other lawful rights over the action corresponding to the mark; other natural persons can also perform the same or similar actions. The mark is not identifiable and cannot clearly refer to the Applicant for Retrial. Therefore, the Applicant for Retrial cannot enjoy the right of portrait over this mark, and his claim that the registration of the disputed trademark harms his right of portrait cannot be established.

Finally, regarding Survey Reports 1 and 2 submitted by the Applicant for Retrial. The survey reports were completed solely by Horizon Company commissioned by the Applicant for Retrial. The attached questions and corresponding conclusions have a certain degree of suggestiveness and speculation, and cannot independently serve as a basis for determining the facts of the case. In the absence of other objective evidence to corroborate, and where the mark " [silhouette figure] " itself does not contain identifiable personal characteristics of the Applicant for Retrial, the two survey reports are insufficient to prove that the Applicant for Retrial's claim is established.

In summary, Michael Jeffrey Jordan's application for retrial does not meet the circumstances provided in Article 91 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 74 of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China," this Court rules as follows:

The application for retrial by Michael Jeffrey Jordan is dismissed.
